lead: Charisma training is the practice of developing the behaviours linked to perceived charisma, such as posture, gestures, vocal delivery, eye contact and warmth, so that other people find you more magnetic and persuasive. In appearance-focused communities it is treated as the behavioural half of looking and presenting well: a person's face and physique set a first impression, and presence is what people say carries it into conversations, dating and work.[1]

Wikipedia reports that research on recordings of speakers, comparisons of people seen as charismatic or not, and experiments indicate that posture, gestures and prosody (the pitch, rhythm and emphasis of the voice) play important roles in perceived charisma, and that some of these behaviours can be taught. It cites a 2011 paper by Antonakis, Fenley and Liechti, 'Can Charisma be Taught? Tests of Two Interventions'.[1]

Popular teaching on the subject includes Olivia Fox Cabane's book The Charisma Myth, which frames charisma as a combination of presence, power and warmth that can be developed as skills rather than a fixed trait.[2] How a person is judged also interacts with appearance: the halo effect and the physical attractiveness stereotype describe the tendency to credit attractive people with more positive traits, which is why many people pair looks work with social-skills work.[3]

chain: Practice posture, gestures, vocal delivery and warmth

angle.text: Charisma training does not change facial structure, but practitioners use it to change how the whole person comes across: upright posture, expressive voice and relaxed eye contact make the same face and physique read as more confident and attractive in person.

paras: The word derives from the Greek charisma, a favour freely given, and was first used for gifts of divine grace. Max Weber adapted it to describe a form of authority, stressing that recognition by those subject to it makes it valid. Scholars such as Paul Joosse describe it as relational, with power resting on followers' attributions.[1] In sociology and management, 'charismatic' also describes a type of leadership.[1]

Wikipedia identifies posture, gestures and prosodic behaviour as the observable elements most associated with perceived charisma, and cites a 2016 acoustic-prosodic analysis of Steve Jobs's speaking voice as an example of vocal research.[1] Cabane's presence-power-warmth model, as summarised on her Wikipedia page, treats charisma as a set of skills; she became known for workshops at the Haas School of Business at UC Berkeley and has been quoted in outlets such as the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times and the BBC.[2]

Psychology describes a halo effect in which a positive impression in one area shapes judgements in others. In a 1972 study by Dion, Berscheid and Walster, 60 students rated photographs and judged attractive people as having more desirable traits and better life outcomes; in a 1974 study by Landy and Sigall, identical essays were rated higher when attributed to an attractive author.[3] Practitioners of looksmaxxing cite this research to argue that appearance and presence reinforce one another.

No studies found on charisma training as a looksmaxxing intervention. In management research, Antonakis, Fenley and Liechti (2011) tested two training interventions in the paper cited by Wikipedia; Wikipedia does not describe the tactics or detailed results.[1]

name: Charisma training

card.summary: Learning the vocal and body-language behaviours associated with charisma; research suggests some can be taught, and few sources tie it to looksmaxxing specifically.
card.note: Sources are thin; looksmaxxing-specific material was not found.

quick.overview:
Charisma training means practising the behaviours people associate with presence, such as posture, gestures and vocal delivery. In appearance-focused circles it is treated as a complement to physical looks.

Wikipedia reports that studies of speakers and experiments show posture, gestures and prosody influence perceived charisma, and that some of these behaviours can be taught.
quick.mechanism: Perceived charisma depends partly on the speaker's nonverbal and vocal behaviour and partly on followers' attributions, following Max Weber's relational view of charisma.
quick.risks: No specific risks are documented. The concept remains ambiguous among scholars.
